title: This Octopus's Mating Arm Detaches and Swims Off on Its Own
subject: argonaut octopus

scenes.text: Science once named a worm. It was an octopus's arm.
The argonaut. The female grows about ten times longer than the male and builds a paper-thin shell to ride near the surface.
The male is barely an inch long. When he finds her, one arm breaks off, swims to her on its own, and stays inside her.
In 1829 the great anatomist Georges Cuvier found those arms inside females and described them as a new parasitic worm.
Decades passed before anyone realised the worm was a piece of a male that had already drifted away.
A worm with no body, an arm with no owner. Only the argonaut.

description:
An argonaut octopus's mating arm detaches, swims to the female on its own and stays inside her.
Female argonauts grow roughly ten times longer than the inch-long males and build a thin, paper-like shell as an egg case. In 1829 Georges Cuvier found the detached arms inside females and named them a new parasitic worm, Hectocotylus; only later did zoologists work out they were part of the male.
Which animal fact fooled scientists the longest?
first_comment: Cuvier was one of the greatest anatomists alive and he still called it a worm. What is the strangest animal body part you know of?
